summary: This note is a Wikipedia-derived overview of Eswatini (called Swaziland in the text), covering its economy, constitution and politics, education, geography, and recent history under the monarchy. It notes the currency peg to the South African Rand, reliance on SACU customs revenue and remittances, and slower growth than neighbours. It also describes the bicameral Parliament, the 1973 suspension of the constitution by King Sobhuza II, and the succession to Mswati III in 1986.
one_line: Overview of Eswatini (Swaziland) covering its economy, monarchy-led politics, parliament, education, geography, and modern history.
key_facts: Swaziland's currency is pegged to the South African Rand, which subsumes Swaziland's monetary policy to South Africa.
Customs duties from the Southern African Customs Union may equal as much as 70% of government revenue this year.
The constitution was put into effect in 2005.
Real GDP growth in Swaziland since 2001 has averaged 2.8%, nearly 2 percentage points lower than other SACU member countries.
The Swazi Parliament, or Libandla, is bicameral, consisting of a Senate with 30 seats and a House of Assembly with 65 seats.
The last parliamentary elections were held on 20 September 2013.
Following the elections of 1973, King Sobhuza II suspended the constitution and thereafter ruled by decree until his death in 1982.
Sobhuza II ruled Swaziland for 61 years, making him the longest ruling monarch in history.
Queen Regent Dzeliwe Shongwe was removed by Liqoqo in 1984 and replaced by Queen Mother Ntfombi Tfwala.
Mswati III, son of Ntfombi, was crowned king on 25 April 1986 as King and Ingwenyama of Swaziland.
Swaziland is a small, landlocked kingdom bordered by the Republic of South Africa on the North, West and South and by Mozambique on the East.
Swaziland has a land area of 17,364 km2 and is located at approximately 26°30'S, 31°30'E.
The Great Usutu River is one of several rivers flowing through the country.
Pre-school education is usually for children 5 years or younger, and 21.6% of preschool age children have access to early childhood education.
Swaziland's public finances deteriorated in the late 1990s following sizeable surpluses a decade earlier.
